title: With me?
description: Do you understand so far?
details:
Example: Are you with me so far?

Usage: A casual comprehension check. Does that make sense? is another option; avoid a tone that sounds like a test.

title: Flat out
description: Very busy.
details:
Example: I’m flat out at work today.

Usage: Informal; in this example it means busy, not lying flat or moving at full speed.

title: Rustle up
description: Make something to eat quickly.
details:
Example: I’ll rustle up some lunch.

Usage: Informal; often used with a quick meal, snack, or whatever food is available.

title: In a rush
description: In a hurry, with little time.
details:
Example: I’m in a rush. Can I call you later?

Usage: Use when you need to do something or leave quickly.

title: Not a single…
description: Not even one.
details:
Example: I haven’t had a single break today.

Usage: Use with a singular noun to emphasise none: not a single seat.

title: Beat the eggs
description: Mix the egg whites and yolks together.
details:
Example: Beat the eggs with a fork.

Usage: A cooking instruction; beat means stir briskly here, not hit.

title: Omelette
description: A dish made by cooking beaten eggs in a pan.
details:
Example: I’m making a cheese omelette.

Usage: Can be plain or have a filling. It isn’t specifically the filling of a tortilla roll.

title: Tortilla
description: A thin, round flatbread used for wraps.
details:
Example: Have we got any tortillas?

Usage: This card uses the flatbread meaning; a Spanish tortilla can mean a thick egg-and-potato dish.

title: Filling
description: The food inside a sandwich, wrap, or pastry.
details:
Example: What filling would you like?

Usage: Here filling is a noun. As an adjective, a filling meal makes you feel full.

title: Dried parsley
description: Parsley preserved as dried flakes for cooking.
details:
Example: Add a little dried parsley.

Usage: A specific cooking ingredient; useful when following a recipe rather than in general small talk.

title: Garlic granules
description: Small dried pieces of garlic used as seasoning.
details:
Example: Can I use garlic granules instead?

Usage: Useful for recipe instructions and ingredient substitutions.

title: Kitchen staples
description: Basic ingredients you keep and use regularly.
details:
Example: Rice and pasta are kitchen staples.

Usage: Store cupboard staples is another British expression for basic ingredients kept at home.

title: Meaty texture
description: A feel when eaten that resembles meat.
details:
Example: These mushrooms have a meaty texture.

Usage: Texture describes how food feels in your mouth, rather than its flavour.

title: Flexible
description: Able to change to suit different needs.
details:
Example: My working hours are flexible.

Usage: Useful for arrangements, schedules, and people. For an ingredient with many uses, versatile is more precise.

title: Flavour boost
description: Something that gives food more flavour.
details:
Example: Lemon juice gives it a flavour boost.

Usage: A cooking phrase; add more flavour is a simpler alternative.

title: Presenter
description: Someone who introduces or leads a programme.
details:
Example: Who’s the presenter of this programme?

Usage: Used in British English for television and radio; host can also work.

title: Pronouns
description: Words such as I, you, she, and they.
details:
Example: The presenter’s cooking. She’s making an omelette.

Usage: A grammar reminder: she refers back to the presenter, so you don’t need to repeat the name or role.

title: Present tense
description: A verb form used for habits, facts, and some summaries.
details:
Example: In the video, she makes a quick lunch.

Usage: The simple present can summarise a video. The past is also possible when recounting what you watched.

title: Salt and pepper
description: Two seasonings often used together.
details:
Example: Could you pass the salt and pepper?

Usage: Pepper is uncountable when referring to the seasoning; peppers can refer to the vegetables.

title: Vocabulary
description: The words someone knows or uses.
details:
Example: I picked up a few new words today.

Usage: When discussing words you learn, say some vocabulary or a few new words, not a few vocabularies.

title: Make a meal
description: Prepare food to eat as a meal.
details:
Example: Let’s make a quick meal before we go.

Usage: Make dinner and make lunch are useful everyday variations.

title: What should I call her?
description: What name or title should I use for her?
details:
Example: What should I call her: Dr Lee or Anna?

Usage: Use when checking how to address someone. For a job or role, ask What does she do?

title: Common fillings
description: Ingredients people often put inside sandwiches or wraps.
details:
Example: What do you usually put in your wraps?

Usage: A practical question about food preferences; you can also ask What’s your favourite filling?

title: Even though
description: Despite the fact that something is true.
details:
Example: Even though I’m tired, I’m going out.

Usage: Use for a real contrast. Don’t add but to the same sentence: Even though I’m tired, but… is incorrect.

title: Summary
description: A short account of the main points.
details:
Example: The video shows how to make a quick lunch.

Usage: A summary leaves out smaller details. Mention the topic and the main points in your own words.

title: Keep it short
description: Use fewer words or take less time.
details:
Example: I’ll keep it short. We need to leave by six.

Usage: Useful for speaking and writing. Include enough information for the other person to understand.
